name: Victor Weber

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for meeting me, Victor. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential. To start, what does a normal working day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work at Oakley Farm for Mr Brandt, three hundred hectares of wheat, barley and sugar beet, and a four-hundred-sow pig unit, which is where I spend most of my time. I'm in the farrowing house by half six, checking the sows that have given birth overnight, making sure the piglets are feeding, moving the weaners on. At harvest I'm on the grain trailer or the beet harvester. It's hard, smelly work and I'm proud of it; the sow mortality's come right down since I took over the farrowing.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live with my partner Katrin, who's a teaching assistant at the primary school in Fenby, in a rented semi-detached house on the edge of the village. We've got about three months of money saved, and I'm on the volunteer fire crew, so my pager goes off at the worst times. The big plan is to get a council starter farm, one of those small farms the county lets to young people, in the next few years. I use an AI app now and then, mainly to check feed numbers and help me write the application.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's like most new things, useful in places, overhyped in others. At the pub I'd say the pigs still need feeding and the fire still needs putting out. I'm not one for posting much online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be pleased, because it means my plan still works. If farming stays roughly as it is, I keep building experience at Oakley and apply for a starter farm in two or three years. The AI app was handy for my application, and that's about all I need from it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep going at Oakley, keep saving, and get the starter farm application in for the next round, which is about eighteen months away. I'd do the farm business course at the college in the evenings, because the council likes to see that. Katrin and I would keep putting a few hundred a month aside.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. It'd feel like the road ahead is still clear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why does the starter farm matter so much to you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My dad was a farm worker all his life and never had his own place. He's sixty now and he still says, if I'd had the chance. I want to be the one in the family who did. And I want our kids, when we have them, to grow up on a farm that's ours, even if it's rented from the council.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you think of the people who've been predicting big changes?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Some of them are selling something, and some genuinely believe it. I don't mind them, I just like to see it working before I believe it. My dad says the same about the weather forecast.

S0.say: I'd say it's like most new things, useful in places and overhyped in others. The pigs still need feeding and the fires still need putting out.
S0.think: I'd be pleased because my plan still works: build experience at Oakley and apply for a council starter farm in two or three years. The AI app helped with my application, and that's all I need from it.
S0.do: Keeps working at Oakley Farm, saves a few hundred a month with his partner and applies for a council starter farm in the round about eighteen months away. Takes the evening farm business course at the college to strengthen the application.
S0.feel: Calm, with the road ahead still clear.
S0.quote: My dad was a farm worker all his life and never had his own place.
S0.fieldNote: Victor's whole outlook is shaped by the goal of a council starter farm and his father's regret at never having one. He's matter-of-fact and proud of his farrowing results. He wants to see things working before he believes in them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the pig industry has been automating for years, with auto feeders and climate control in the sheds, so this is more of the same. At the pub I'd say the good stockmen will still be needed. I'd also say people should learn a trade properly, not just expect a job to be handed to them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'd be fine, mostly. The feeding and the ventilation are already done by computers at Oakley, and they still need me for the sows and the piglets, which is skilled work. If anything, a bit more automation would make a starter farm easier to run on my own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd watch what other pig units brought in, and once something was clearly working, I'd ask Mr Brandt to try it and offer to learn it. I'd use the AI app a bit more, maybe for the records, once I'd seen others do it. And I'd keep saving for the starter farm, maybe a bit more each month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, really. Maybe a bit curious.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you need to see before trusting a new machine in the farrowing house?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A whole year of it on someone else's unit, with the piglet numbers to prove it. A camera that spots a sow lying on her piglets would be brilliant, if it worked. But I've seen things that promised the world and then needed three engineers to keep running.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is anyone at Oakley more at risk than you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sam, who does the washing and cleaning of the pens between batches. There are already robots that pressure-wash pig pens. He's nineteen and he's a good lad, so I'd tell him to start learning the sows with me, so he's got something they can't easily replace.

S1.say: I'd say the pig industry has automated for years with feeders and climate control, so this is more of the same and good stockmen will still be needed. People should learn a trade properly.
S1.think: I think I'd be fine, since computers already run the feeding and ventilation and they still need me for the sows. More automation might even make a starter farm easier to run alone.
S1.do: Watches what other pig units bring in and, once something clearly works, asks his boss to try it and offers to learn it. Uses the AI app more for records once he's seen others do it, and saves a bit more for the starter farm.
S1.quote: I've seen things that promised the world and then needed three engineers to keep running.
S1.fieldNote: Victor treats steady change as normal for the pig industry and even sees it helping his starter farm plan. He sets a clear test of a year's piglet numbers before trusting a machine. His instinct is to pull a younger colleague into skilled stock work, an apprenticeship in all but name.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is too fast for anyone to handle well, and people need to look after their own families and communities first. I'd want the government to keep it fair, but not just hand money out; help people get into new work. I'd say it at the fire station, where we all talk about everything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the starter farm plan would be finished. If robots can run a pig unit or an arable farm better than me in two years, why would the council give a small farm to a young lad with a certificate? Or if they did, how would I compete with a company running ten farms with robots?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd pull out of spending on anything big, and keep our three months safe. I'd talk to Katrin about putting the starter farm off and maybe looking at buying a house instead while prices are uncertain. At Oakley I'd stay as long as Mr Brandt wanted me, and I'd ask the fire service whether there's paid work, because I'd want something steady with people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Mostly about the dream going, more than the job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your dad about the starter farm?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's the hard one. I'd probably say we'll wait and see, which is what he'd say. But we'd both know. He'd go quiet and then ask about the pigs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd want something steady with people. Why the fire service?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because when your house is on fire, you want a person at the door, not a machine. Maybe that's not true by 2028 either, I don't know. But it's the thing I'd bet on.

S2.say: I'd say it's too fast to handle well, and people should look after their families and communities first. The government should keep it fair by helping people into new work, not just handing out money.
S2.think: I think the starter farm plan would be finished, because the council wouldn't give a small farm to a young worker if robots run farms better. And I couldn't compete with a company running ten robot farms.
S2.do: Stops any big spending and protects their three months of savings. Discusses dropping the starter farm plan with his partner, stays at Oakley as long as he's wanted, and asks the fire service about paid work.
S2.feel: Anxious, mostly about losing his dream rather than the job.
S2.quote: He'd go quiet and then ask about the pigs.
S2.fieldNote: For Victor, the fast scenario hurts most because it ends the plan to have his own farm, and with it his father's hopes. He still frames support as help into new work rather than payments. The fire service is his best bet for work that people will still want a person to do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough for people who are willing to work and learn. I'd tell the younger lads at the fire station to pick something practical and get good at it. I'd want the council to keep the starter farms going, because those are about community, not just food.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think it'd change my plan rather than kill it. If I got a starter farm in two or three years, I'd have to run it with the new machines from the start, and that might actually work for one person. It's a gamble, though, and I'm not a big gambler.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd watch the first year closely, especially what the robot pen washers and farrowing cameras do on other units. I'd still apply for the starter farm, but with a plan that uses the new kit once it's proven, and I'd use the AI app to help me put the numbers together. We'd try to get the savings to five or six months before taking the tenancy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but I'd have something to aim at.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you're not a big gambler. What would make you take the tenancy anyway?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If I'd seen two or three young farmers round here doing it with robots and making it pay. Not on a video, here, in the county. Then it's not much of a gamble anymore, is it?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does Katrin make of the plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She's careful, more than me. She'd want her job at the school as our steady money while I took the risk. That's fair. Kids will still need a teaching assistant to tie their shoelaces and calm them down, I'd hope.

S3.say: I'd say five years is enough for people willing to work and learn, and young people should pick something practical and get good at it. The council should keep starter farms going because they're about community.
S3.think: It'd change my plan rather than end it, because a starter farm run with new machines from the start might work for one person. It's still a gamble, and I'm not a big gambler.
S3.do: Watches the first year closely, especially robot pen washers and farrowing cameras on other units. Still applies for a starter farm with a plan to use proven machines, uses the AI app for the numbers, and builds savings to five or six months before taking the tenancy.
S3.feel: Uneasy but with a goal to aim at.
S3.quote: Not on a video, here, in the county.
S3.fieldNote: Five years turns Victor's dream into a calculated plan that includes the new machines. He'd only commit after seeing local young farmers make it pay. His partner's steady job is part of the plan, and he still values community over pure efficiency.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a fair amount of time, so there's no reason for anyone to be caught napping. Farmers have always adapted, from horses to tractors to computers. Learn what works and get on with it, that's what I'd say.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, I'd see it as a good run-up. I could get the starter farm, run it for a few years the normal way, and bring the robots in once they've proven themselves. I'd be thirty-seven when it fully arrives, with my own farm, hopefully, and maybe a couple of kids.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd apply for the starter farm in the next round and do the business course. Katrin and I would probably get married and think about a family, because ten years is too long to put life on hold. Once machines had been proven on other farms for a couple of years, I'd buy or lease them for my own place, carefully, one at a time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, a little, but mostly calm. It's a long enough road to plan properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything about the ten-year picture that bothers you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Whether there's still a reason for the council to let small farms at the end of it. If robots make big farms that cheap, maybe they sell the land instead. I'd want to have my feet under the table by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you hope your dad sees in ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Me on my own yard, with my name on the gate. Even if a robot's doing half the work, I'd want him to stand there and know it's ours. That'd be enough for both of us.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is fair warning, so nobody should be caught napping. Farmers have always adapted, from horses to tractors to computers, so learn what works and get on with it.
S4.think: I'd see it as a good run-up: get the starter farm, run it normally for a few years and bring in robots once proven. At thirty-seven I'd hopefully have my own farm and maybe children.
S4.do: Applies for a starter farm in the next round and does the business course. Marries his partner and plans a family, and once machines have been proven on other farms for a couple of years, buys or leases them one at a time for his own place.
S4.feel: Mostly calm with a little unease, because it's a long road to plan.
S4.quote: Even if a robot's doing half the work, I'd want him to stand there and know it's ours.
S4.fieldNote: With ten years, Victor fits the change into his existing plan: get the farm first, then add proven machines. His remaining worry is whether councils will still let small farms. The image of his father at the farm gate shows what's really at stake for him.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because it ends the starter farm before I've even started. What would help is the council keeping starter farms going and helping young tenants buy the new machines, like a loan or a shared scheme. Proper apprenticeships for the new kit too, not just online courses.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe the fire crew and things like that. In a village, a lot of what keeps us going isn't paid work at all. If people lose their jobs and move away, there's nobody to answer the pager. That matters as much as the farms.

headlineQuote: If people lose their jobs and move away, there's nobody to answer the pager.
portrait: Victor Weber is 27 and runs the farrowing side of a 400-sow pig unit on Oakley Farm, an arable and pig farm, living in a rented house with his partner Katrin, a teaching assistant. He volunteers on the fire crew and dreams of a council starter farm so he can have the place his farm-worker father never had. He uses AI now and then and wants to see a full year's results before trusting any machine. Steady change leaves him calm, but two-year AGI makes him anxious because it would end the starter farm dream. With five or ten years he plans to take the tenancy and add proven robots one at a time.
biggestWorry: AGI in two years, because it would end his plan for a council starter farm before he had even begun.
whatWouldHelp: Councils keeping starter farms going and helping young tenants afford new machines through loans or shared schemes, plus proper apprenticeships for the new equipment.
